title: From Sight‐Reading to Practiced Performance: Characterizing Upper‐Body Kinematics in Expert Pianists Using Markerless Motion Capture
content:
Markerless motion capture was used to quantify upper-body kinematics in expert pianists during initial sight-reading and performance following brief practice/familiarization. Practice was associated with fewer direction changes in selected joint-angle trajectories, indicating fewer trajectory reversals during performance. These findings demonstrate measurable short-term changes in upper-body kinematics as pianists become familiar with novel musical material and illustrate the application of markerless motion capture in ecologically relevant piano-performance research.


ABSTRACT

Sight-reading on the piano demands rapid spatiotemporal adjustments in movement patterns, yet its biomechanical basis and immediate practice effects remain underexplored. We characterized upper-body kinematics in expert pianists across two ecologically related performance states: initial sight-reading of unfamiliar musical material and performance of the same material following brief practice/familiarization. Twenty expert pianists performed two excerpts: a rapid scale-like (dexterous) task and a repetitive chordal task, followed by up to 10 min of practice. Movements were recorded at 120 Hz using eight cameras and a markerless motion capture system (Theia3D), yielding shoulder-, elbow-, and wrist-angle trajectories. The number of direction changes, a position-domain measure of trajectory reversals, was the primary outcome; range of motion (ROM) and median angular velocity were secondary outcomes. Short practice was associated with fewer direction changes in selected upper-body joint-angle trajectories in both tasks, with more widespread changes in the chordal task. No significant practice-related changes in ROM or median angular velocity were observed after correcting for multiple comparisons. These findings demonstrate measurable short-term changes in upper-body joint-angle trajectories between initial sight-reading and performance following brief practice and illustrate the application of markerless motion capture to the study of ecologically relevant, unconstrained piano performance.
